title: A little 1954 magic in Buenos Aires.
summary: Photos of Don Julio in Palermo, Buenos Aires, and the sweet 1954 tradition Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve share before their Viking cruise.
search: Home/The journal/Buenos Aires Buenos Aires, Argentina · From the family camera rollA little 1954 magic in Buenos Aires.Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve, a famous restaurant, and a very special number.A family travel note · October 2026One happy stop in Buenos Aires before the next adventure at sea. Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve are off on another adventure! Before boarding their Viking cruise, they made a stop at Don Julio in Buenos Aires — a restaurant recommended by my colleagues in Argentina.And what a gorgeous place for a photograph. Green-and-white striped awnings, a beautiful old building, and pumpkins everywhere. They look almost like New England in October, even though it's spring in Buenos Aires.But one of my favorite pictures from this stop isn't of the restaurant at all. Another 1954 for their collection.Their little travel tradition1954.Mom-Mom and Steve were both born in 1954. Wherever they travel, if they spot that number on a building, sign, or street address, they take a photograph.A small souvenir from every place they find it. I love that they have this tradition — a little reminder of the year they both came into the world.Of all the things you can collect while traveling, I think this might be one of the sweetest. ❤️ A little adventure of their own.These two give so much love and time to James and their other grandchildren. They're part of the family village that makes so many of our days possible, particularly when life involves the extra planning and support James needs.They also love to travel. And I love seeing them out exploring together, doing something for themselves, collecting stories (and 1954s) along the way.Oh, and don't worry: Ruby was in very good hands while they were away. 🐾 The Don Julio storefront on a beautiful sunny day.Pumpkins in springtime, Buenos Aires style. A little connection back homeA taste of Argentina, by way of Maine.Speaking of Buenos Aires: if you'd like a taste of Argentina a little closer to home, Rococo Ice Cream in Kennebunk, Maine, has its own Argentine connection. Its founder spent time in Argentina, where the city's ice-cream culture helped inspire what became one of our family's favorite New England stops.Read our family's Rococo story, A scoop with a view → We have lots more to share from Mom-Mom and Steve's South American travels. For now, here's to a beautiful stop at Don Julio, a recommendation from colleagues halfway around the world, and another little piece of 1954 to add to the collection.May they find a thousand more. ❤️❤️ The 1954 photo tradition Have you ever found your year? Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve look for 1954 wherever they go. An old doorway, a date carved into a building, a street number in another country. It is such a little thing, and such a lovely way to remember a place. Were you born in 1954, too? Have you ever stopped to photograph your own birth year, an anniversary or another number that means something to you? I'd love to hear what you've found. title: Burlington, at our pace.
summary: Our Burlington, Vermont trip in family photographs: Oakledge’s accessible treehouse, pool time at The Essex, Al’s French Frys, and a little holiday sparkle.
search: The journal / Vermont Burlington & Essex, Vermont · From the family album Burlington, at our pace. A treehouse, a swim, a stop at Al’s, and a little holiday sparkle. The small pieces of a Vermont trip worth keeping. Published October 16, 2026 · Photographs from an earlier family trip Pool time at The Essex. One of the good parts of getting away. The little storyThe treehouseOur Al’s stopAccess & planningUseful links Looking back through our Burlington photographs, I keep coming back to the smaller scenes: James in his Vermont shirt, the red booths at Al’s, a tree growing straight through a treehouse, and the two of them together in the pool. There is a very good Vermont trip in those pictures. A little time outside. Something familiar to eat. Water to get into. A Christmas tree dressed in black-and-white checks, because apparently even the decorations had packed appropriately. For our family, those ordinary pieces deserve room in the story. James loves the water, and the swimming photographs belong right alongside the sightseeing ones. The pool is part of the trip. A swim at The Essex The indoor pool at The Essex Resort & Spa has a lovely setting: wood walls, white beams, large windows, and blue-green water. In our photographs, James is wearing his life jacket with his dad beside him. In another, the two of them are wrapped up in a poolside hug. The photograph I would keep even without a travel story attached.White robes, white columns, and a little Vermont sunshine. The covered walkway is another detail I like in the album: two white robes, a long row of columns, and stripes of sunlight across the path. It is a useful reminder to ask about the journey between a room and a pool. The Essex’s spa is in a separate building; the practical notes below include the resort’s current access information. A treehouse you can actually get into At Oakledge Park in Burlington, the treehouse is built around the tree itself. Thick branches frame the view; the floorboards and rustic railings make a little room in the woods. James’s orange jacket stands out against all that weathered wood. Inside Oakledge’s treehouse, with the tree very much part of the room.A place to stop and look out. The access is part of what makes this place worth knowing about. Its builders describe it as a universally accessible community treehouse, created with the City of Burlington. That matters: the experience of being up among the branches should have room for more people. Our photographs capture the inside, rather than the full approach. For a future visit, I would check the route and current conditions with the park, especially after wet or icy weather. A lovely wooden walkway still has to contend with Vermont. Red booths and a Vermont shirt Our stop at Al’s French Frys in South Burlington looks exactly like the sort of place you hope to find on a New England trip: red booths, little pendant lights, and a black-and-white tiled floor. James is standing by the table in his Vermont shirt, with his device close by. A Vermont shirt for a Vermont stop. Al’s French Frys, South Burlington. That is a useful little travel detail in its own right. A communication device belongs at the table, within reach. New surroundings need not mean leaving familiar supports behind. Al’s current menu lists its namesake fries alongside burgers, sandwiches, and ice cream. The photo is our souvenir of the stop; for a particular food preference or allergy, check the current menu and preparation details directly. A little holiday sparkle A grin, red ornaments, and rather good checked ribbon. And then there is this picture. James, smiling beside the Christmas tree, blue Crocs and all. The ribbon is coordinated. The family travel wardrobe is taking a more independent approach. Looking through this trip again, what stands out is the variety without the need for a grand production: the treehouse, the pool, the diner, the decorations. There is plenty here for a family album, and plenty to build a manageable Burlington visit around. Take the useful details with youPlanning your own version These are memories from an earlier trip. The venue details below were checked on October 16, 2026; they describe what the venues currently publish, rather than facilities we personally tested. The Essex Resort & Spa · 70 Essex Way, EssexThe resort lists a year-round indoor pool. Its accessibility page says the spa and fitness center are in a separate building with paved wheelchair access, and that the pools and whirlpool have lifts. Ask about the exact route from your room, lift availability, changing arrangements, and current family swimming hours. We did not test the lifts or accessible rooms. Oakledge Park · Flynn Avenue, BurlingtonThe treehouse is documented as a universally accessible community treehouse. Burlington’s parks guidance says it is first come, first served and must remain open to the public. Burlington Wildways lists parking and accessible spaces near the Greenway. Check current parking charges, restroom availability, and the condition of the treehouse approach before you go. Al’s French Frys · 1251 Williston Road, South BurlingtonOur photo shows indoor booth seating. It does not establish wheelchair clearance, restroom access, or typical sound levels. Call 802-862-9203 for the seating or access details your family needs, and check the current menu and hours. A simple plan Choose one main outing, leave room for swimming, and keep a food stop flexible. These places are in Burlington, South Burlington, and Essex, so allow for driving between them. The photographs are a collection of trip moments, not a timed itinerary. For us, a useful planning question is: what does everyone need in order to enjoy the part we came for? A place to change, a device within reach, time to linger, and permission to finish while the day is still going well. Our hotel and pool checklist can help with the calls before booking. For a shorter outing, start with the shorter-visit plan. title: Almost home.
summary: A decade in Burlington, a return from Massachusetts with James, and South Burlington’s whale tails: memories, parking, walking access and nearby I-89.
search: The journal / Vermont South Burlington, Vermont · From the family album Almost home.Burlington’s whale tails, then and now. A decade of lake days, friendship and belonging—and a return from Massachusetts with James. With parking, walking access and nearby-highway planning notes. An AUsome Life · Published October 22, 2026 · A memory from an earlier family visit James at the whale tails. An old sign of home, and a new family memory. The storyParking & walking accessHighway & elopement planningMore photographs & sources For years, two whale tails sticking out of a Vermont field meant I was almost home. I lived in Burlington for a decade, and Lake Champlain was my everything. Being near the water brought me peace and helped ease my anxiety. I could look out over the lake and feel a little more room inside myself. That kind of comfort stays with you. My friends were just as much a part of what made it home. When I think about Burlington, the people and the place come together: the friendships, the lake, the feeling of belonging to a community. It is a community like no other I’ve known, surrounded by a beauty I still miss. That is what the whale tails were welcoming me back to. There they were beside I-89, familiar and wonderfully improbable. I couldn’t tell you how many times I passed them over those years. I can tell you what seeing them meant: nearly there. Back to the lake, my friends, my life. They are technically in South Burlington, but to me they belong to that feeling of arriving in Burlington. Two enormous whale tails in the grass. In Vermont. Of course. They are so perfectly Burlington: art out in the open, a little oddness, a love of the natural world, and something worth looking at on an otherwise ordinary drive. I love that they manage to be both a surprise and an old friend. Now home is in Massachusetts. Getting back to Vermont takes a little more doing, and being able to make that trek with James means a great deal to me. There is something wonderful about bringing your child to a place that already holds years of your life. You arrive with all those memories, and then you get to add him. That is what I see in this photograph. James on the green path, smiling, with tall grasses on either side and the whale tails up behind him. All that blue sky. A place I have carried around in my mind, with my son right there in the middle of it. For so long, the tails were something I passed on my way home. Getting out and walking toward them with James made them a destination in their own right. I love having a photograph of that. When I think of the whale tails now, I get to think of this day, too. The sculpture has a proper name: Reverence. Jim Sardonis created it in 1989, carving the tails from African black granite. They spent their first ten years in Randolph before moving to South Burlington in 1999. At roughly 12 to 13 feet high, they have a presence that a passing glimpse from the highway doesn’t quite convey.1, 2 And there really is a whale story beneath the Vermont landscape. The Champlain Valley was once occupied by the Champlain Sea. In 1849, railroad workers in nearby Charlotte uncovered the bones of a beluga whale. The University of Vermont tells the story of that discovery and the ancient sea that explains it.3 Whales in a Vermont field turn out to be a little less improbable than they first appear. I appreciate that history. I appreciate the sculpture. But my attachment to those tails is also very simple: I saw them over the years, and they came to mean home. Massachusetts is home now, too. Coming back with James lets those two parts of my life meet. I get to bring him into a place that gave me so much: friendship, beauty, and somewhere to find a little peace. I can be a visitor here and still feel the old recognition. There they are. I know this place. And now I have this picture of James to add to all the years before it. The practical detailsVisiting the whale tails Our photograph records an earlier visit. These planning notes were checked on October 22, 2026, using the artist’s directions, Technology Park and Trail Finder. Conditions and parking arrangements can change. Where to go & parkReverence is at Technology Park in South Burlington. Approach via Community Drive off Kimball Avenue; Trail Finder places the trailhead on the right as the road curves. Use designated trail parking and follow posted signs. Reach the walking route through Technology Park. Cost & walking distanceTrail Finder lists no fee and a 1.7-mile loop. That is the full listed loop, not a measured parking-to-sculpture distance. A Vermont Moms account describes a shorter walk directly to the tails. Follow the current marked route and turn back when it suits your family. Ground & mobility accessThe listed surfaces are grass/meadow and packed earth/dirt. Our photo shows the uphill grassy approach. Trail Finder rates the route “easy,” but wheelchair and stroller suitability depends on the device, slope and ground conditions. A paved accessible route, accessible parking bays and visitor toilets were not confirmed in the sources checked. Comfort & planningOur photo shows an exposed stretch with little shade. Bring water and weather protection, and allow for softer or slippery ground after rain or snow. With the interstate nearby, traffic sound is a reasonable planning consideration. Ask Technology Park about the current route and any access details your family needs. A separate note for the visitThe highway, the distance & elopement planning Yes—when you drive past the whale tails on I-89, you are on the interstate. That wonderfully unexpected highway glimpse was my sign that I was almost home. Technology Park places them between exits 12 and 13. To visit on foot, leave the highway and use the park’s trail approach. Do not stop on the interstate shoulder or try to walk in from I-89. How close is the highway? Roughly 100 feet (30 metres) from the sculptures to the nearest paved edge of northbound I-89. This is our straight-line estimate from 2024 Vermont aerial imagery, checked for this story—not a surveyed distance, a walking route or a safety buffer. It is also entirely separate from the distance you walk from parking. For a family planning around elopement or wandering, that proximity deserves attention. The CDC describes wandering as leaving a safe area or responsible caregiver, and identifies traffic as a danger. It can happen even with attentive supervision. This is a planning consideration, not a report of an incident on our visit. Boundary fencing appears in reference photographs, but we have not verified its present condition or a continuous barrier around the walking area. Treat this as an outdoor trail beside a highway, rather than an enclosed play space. Plan the close support your child needs before leaving the car, agree who is staying with them during photographs, keep familiar communication supports available, and make room for “break” or “all done.” The photograph can wait. If the setting does not suit your family that day, the passing view from a safely driven car can be the whole experience. There is no need to turn an old sign of home into an outing that asks too much. More views & useful reading For more photographs, see Jim Sardonis’s official Reverence gallery and Trail Finder’s photographs and trail map, including a winter view. The photograph of James above is from our family collection. Technology Park: The Story of the Whales Tails — location, dimensions and history.
